nodes.title: Ultrafast isomerization initiated by X-ray core ionization
nodes.main_claim: X-ray core ionization initiates ultrafast isomerization of acetylene dication (C₂D₂²⁺) to vinylidene on a timescale of ~12 fs or faster, with significant proton redistribution occurring during the core-hole lifetime (~6 fs) before Auger relaxation completes, thereby requiring modification of conventional transition-state theory that neglects geometry evolution during core ionization.

nodes.description: Proton migration in acetylene dication is a key model system for understanding isomerization driven by nonadiabatic electron-nuclear interactions in hydrocarbons, with applications to radiation damage in biomolecular X-ray imaging.

Previous synchrotron measurements (Osipov et al.) established an upper limit of <60 fs for X-ray-initiated isomerization timescale, which is unexpectedly fast compared to transition-state theory predictions of picosecond timescales based on calculated barrier heights (~2.3 eV) and expected vibrational excitation levels.

The mechanism underlying this ultrafast isomerization could not be directly probed by previous non-time-resolved measurements, motivating a time-resolved X-ray pump/X-ray probe experiment to directly detect geometry changes in the time domain.

Optical laser experiments show isomerization timescales of ~90 fs when initiated by strong-field 800 nm radiation, but core ionization (weak-field regime) produces different electronic state distributions and vibrational excitations than strong-field ionization, potentially enabling different isomerization mechanisms.

Deuterated acetylene (C₂D₂²⁺) rather than C₂H₂²⁺ was used to eliminate background proton contamination; if isomerization rate is limited by nuclear mass, deuterium should show slower dynamics than hydrogen.

Experimental strategy: First X-ray pulse (400 eV, ~10 fs) core-ionizes carbon K-shell, creating a dication in a non-stationary superposition of electronic states with different vibrational excitations; second X-ray pulse at variable delay further ionizes to tetracation (C₂D₂⁴⁺), which dissociates and reveals instantaneous molecular geometry via fragment momentum analysis.

nodes.description: When a core-ionized carbon atom creates a sudden change in the Coulomb field, the adjacent deuteron experiences an impulse that initiates its motion before Auger relaxation occurs; this geometry change during the ~6 fs core-hole lifetime has been typically neglected in core ionization analysis.

For light nuclei (deuterons/protons), the geometry change during the core-hole lifetime may not be negligible, unlike for heavier nuclei or atoms with fast Auger relaxation rates; the deuteron can acquire non-negligible momentum that persists after Auger relaxation.

Calculations of the core-excited singly-charged ion (C₂D₂⁺*) show that the vibrational constant for the bending mode decreases compared to neutral acetylene, and anharmonicity leads to broadening of the vibrational wavepacket during the core-hole lifetime.

The dication is created in an initial geometry different from neutral ground-state acetylene, and both the geometry change and acquired momentum during the core-hole lifetime modify the path towards isomerization.

Franck-Condon overlaps between neutral and dication states must account for both geometry changes and acquired momentum during the core-hole lifetime to correctly estimate kinetic energy available for surmounting the isomerization barrier.

Transition-state theory applied to the dication potential energy surface alone is insufficient to describe the observed ultrafast isomerization because the initial state excited by core ionization is not static but evolves during the core-hole lifetime.

Time-resolved X-ray pump/X-ray probe experiments with four-particle coincident detection enable direct probing of molecular dynamics initiated by core ionization, creating 'molecular movies' of evolving geometry.

Nonadiabatic interactions couple nuclear motion into the electronic relaxation process in the first tens of femtoseconds following core ionization, and geometry changes during core excitation must be accounted for to understand early-time dynamics in core ionization of species with light nuclei.

These findings have important implications for understanding hydrocarbon isomerization and radiation damage by intense X-ray radiation, particularly for diffraction-before-destroy measurements of biomolecular structure at X-ray FELs.

nodes.description: Illustrates the excitation scheme showing how the 4+ charge state is formed through sequential core ionization and Auger decay from the pump and probe pulses, contrasting with alternative ionization pathways
nodes.excerpt: The first X-ray pulse core ionizes the acetylene molecule, which, in the dominant relaxation channel, subsequently loses a second electron via Auger decay (see Fig. 1). The dication is created in a non-stationary state, a superposition of many electronic states, each with a different degree of vibrational excitation. The relaxation that follows initiates the geometrical change that can lead to isomerization and molecular breakup. On a variable delay a second X-ray pulse, with the same characteristics as the first one, probes the instantaneous geometry in the relaxing dication by further core ionization and Auger decay. The result is C₂D₂⁴⁺, which has no bound states.

nodes.description: Describes how alternative ionization paths (shake ionization and L-shell ionization) lead to different final charge states, making them distinguishable from the desired 4+ channel
nodes.location: Results - Strategy for the ultrafast X-ray probe section
nodes.excerpt: Alternative direct and shake ionization paths that involve the L-shell of carbon typically lead to a different final charge state than the 4+ channel. A combination of a loss of three electrons through a shake process in one step, and a loss of one electron in L-shell ionization in another step, would lead to the final state of 4+. This combination is at least two orders of magnitude less likely than the excitation path discussed in the text.
